name: CoolSculpting (cryolipolysis)

card.summary: Controlled cold applied to a patch of fat to reduce it without surgery; studies show modest local reductions and a rare paradoxical-growth risk.
card.note: Reduction is modest and localized, not weight loss; rare paradoxical adipose hyperplasia (about 0.12 to 1.0 percent in reports) can require surgery to correct.

quick.overview:
Cryolipolysis cools a section of subcutaneous fat with an applicator to a temperature intended to injure fat cells while sparing skin. The body then clears the damaged cells over the following weeks. CoolSculpting is the best-known brand.

Systematic reviews report modest reductions in fat-layer thickness in treated areas, with high satisfaction. Forum members have discussed it as a way to reduce local fat, including the chin and cheeks.
quick.mechanism: Fat cells are more sensitive to cold than the overlying skin. Controlled cooling is thought to trigger apoptosis-like fat-cell injury and gradual removal by the body, shown in pig experiments published in 2009.
quick.risks: Common effects are redness, numbness, swelling, bruising and mild pain, usually resolving within weeks. Paradoxical adipose hyperplasia, in which treated fat enlarges, has been reported at roughly 0.12 to 1.0 percent and can require liposuction or abdominoplasty to treat.

lead: Cryolipolysis, often called fat freezing, is a non-invasive procedure that uses controlled cooling of subcutaneous fat for localized fat reduction. For people working on their appearance it targets a discrete bulge that diet and training have left in place, such as a lower-abdomen roll, flank, bra-line area or the fat beneath the chin, so that the contour of the body or jawline looks leaner. The term is frequently used interchangeably with the brand name CoolSculpting, introduced in the United States in 2010 by Zeltiq Aesthetics and acquired by Allergan Aesthetics in 2017 [1][16]. The FDA has cleared it for several body areas including the submental area, jawline, arms, flanks, abdomen and thighs [1].

The technology was licensed from Massachusetts General Hospital and developed commercially by a company founded in 2005 as Juniper Medical and renamed Zeltiq in 2007; Allergan bought Zeltiq in February 2017 for about 2.48 billion dollars [16]. Early pig and human studies were published in 2009 [5][7].

Systematic reviews have reported modest effects. A 2015 review of 19 studies found skinfold thickness reductions of 10.3 to 28.5 percent with high patient satisfaction, and a 2023 review of 18 studies reported ultrasound-measured fat reductions of 2.0 to 5.1 mm and judged the treatment safe but modestly effective, with low-quality data [1]. A 2025 meta-analysis of 30 studies and 3,158 participants reported pooled reductions in abdominal circumference and suprailiac fat thickness 12 weeks after treatment and a satisfaction rate of 80.4 percent [17]. Reviews also describe a rare complication, paradoxical adipose hyperplasia, which came to wide public attention when the model Linda Evangelista said she had experienced it [1][18].

On looksmax.org the procedure has been described as a way to cause local fat loss, including a thread proposing it for facial fat pockets [4]; T Nation members have asked about it for stubborn spots and as a way to remove fat cells permanently [19][20].

chain: Applicator cools a targeted fat bulge
Treated fat cells are injured and cleared over weeks to months
Thinner fat layer and a more defined local contour
angle.text: Patients use cryolipolysis to thin a discrete fat pocket, most often the abdomen, flanks, thighs, arms or the area under the chin, without surgery or recovery time. Results appear gradually over several months, and the procedure is used on localized fat rather than for general weight loss.

paras: Cryolipolysis applies controlled cold to a section of tissue, usually drawn between or against cooling applicators. The premise is that subcutaneous fat is more vulnerable to cold than the overlying skin. A pig-model study published in Dermatologic Surgery in 2009 examined whether controlled cooling could selectively damage subcutaneous fat without injuring overlying skin and surrounding structures or raising lipid levels; it used three Yucatan pigs treated at 22 sites [5].

A 2023 review describes the cooled fat cells as undergoing apoptosis, with the damaged cells then removed by macrophages, producing a thinner fat layer over time [15]. A review in Lasers in Surgery and Medicine summarized the preclinical and clinical evidence on mechanism, efficacy and safety [6]. A human study in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery treated ten subjects with a prototype cooling device and examined whether the treatment affects local sensory function or nerve fibers [7].

A 2025 randomized trial examined the effects of cryolipolysis on subcutaneous adipose tissue of adult women using immunohistochemical analysis [9], and a 2025 pilot randomized study looked at whether it converts white adipose tissue [21]. A 2023 review of future directions describes new applicator designs, combination therapies and an injectable ice-slurry approach under development [10].

Zeltiq's founder, Mitch Levinson, who had previously led the radio-frequency skin-tightening company Thermage, started the company in 2005 as Juniper Medical; it was renamed Zeltiq in July 2007, and it licensed cryolipolysis patents from Massachusetts General Hospital [16]. Pig-model results were published in 2009 [5], followed by early human efficacy studies [7].

In 2010 the FDA cleared the device for skin cooling before dermatology procedures and later that year for fat removal at the flanks; abdominal clearance followed in 2012, and a model without a suction cup was cleared for thighs in 2014 [16]. Zeltiq raised 75 million dollars across four funding rounds by the end of 2010 and went public in 2011, raising 91 million dollars [16]. Allergan acquired the company in February 2017, and AbbVie in turn acquired Allergan in 2020 [16]. A 2013 article gave a broad overview of clinical and commercial experience with the device [12].

The FDA clearances cover the submental area, jawline, upper arms, back and bra line, lumbar rolls, flanks, abdomen, thighs and under the buttocks [1][16]. A study of submental fat examined safety and efficacy of the technique under the chin [8], and a review of nonsurgical neck rejuvenation lists cryolipolysis among options for submental fat, alongside percutaneous radiofrequency, radiofrequency-helium plasma and deoxycholic acid injections; in that review percutaneous radiofrequency had the highest patient satisfaction and lowest complication rate [3][14].

The Wikipedia article on fat removal procedures describes cryolipolysis as best suited to limited, discrete fat bulges and contrasts it with liposuction, which removes fat with a cannula and has a downtime of two to four weeks or more [18]. An Aesthetic Surgery Journal trial of cryolipolysis for fat on the lateral chest wall after mastectomy has also been published [22].

Reviews summarised on Wikipedia report skinfold reductions of 10.3 to 28.5 percent (2015, 19 studies) and ultrasound fat-thickness reductions of 2.0 to 5.1 mm (2023, 18 studies), with the latter noting low data quality [1]. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis in Obesity Reviews included 30 studies and 3,158 participants and reported lower body mass index (mean difference -1.80), waist-to-hip ratio, abdominal circumference (-3.56 cm) and suprailiac fat thickness (-5.22 mm) 12 weeks after treatment compared with baseline [17].

Studies have used three-dimensional volumetric measurement of fat loss [11] and a split-body trial examined changes in abdominal visceral and subcutaneous fat 12 weeks after a single unilateral session [13]. A 2023 randomized split-body trial reported that active heating after cryolipolysis reduced efficacy and side effects [23]. A review of noninvasive subcutaneous fat reduction compared cryolipolysis with other methods [2], and a broader 2024 narrative review covered cryolipolysis among body contouring technologies including ultrasound, radiofrequency and shock wave [24].
Reviewers cited above describe the changes as modest and describe treatment as aimed at localized fat rather than weight reduction [1][18].

Common effects include redness, numbness, swelling, bruising and mild pain, usually resolving within weeks [1]. A 2013 study examined safety, tolerance and patient satisfaction [25]. The 2025 meta-analysis reported an adverse-event rate of 49.5 percent across included studies, alongside an 80.4 percent satisfaction rate [17].

Paradoxical adipose hyperplasia (PAH), in which the treated fat enlarges, has been reported in about 0.12 to 1.0 percent of treatments and has been treated with liposuction or abdominoplasty [1]. Wikipedia notes that because patients often receive multiple treatments, the rate per patient may be higher than the per-treatment figure [18]. A case report has also described morphea, a localized skin hardening, after cryolipolysis [26].

In September 2021 Linda Evangelista said that a CoolSculpting treatment about five years earlier had caused PAH and that this was why she had stepped away from work; she sued Zeltiq for 50 million dollars, and the case was settled in July 2022 on undisclosed terms [16][27].

Human studies include a systematic review of clinical data on efficacy and safety [2], a literature review [6], studies of submental fat [8], volumetric quantification of fat loss [11], and a study of effects on peripheral nerves [7]. A randomized trial of systemic effects in centrally obese women has also been reported [28].

Registered trials include a phase 4 trial of safety and efficacy of cryolipolysis protocols in 395 people (NCT06541899) [29], one of cryolipolysis combined with aerobic exercise for abdominal fat [30], one of cryolipolysis combined with a radiofrequency device for the flanks [31], one on cellulite combined with subcision [32] and one comparing ultrasound lipolysis with cryolipolysis on lipid profile in centrally obese men [33]. Wikipedia describes the evidence overall as moderate in effect, with low data quality in the most recent review [1].

A looksmax.org thread presents fat freezing as a local fat-loss method, proposes that cooled fat cells turn into brown fat that burns calories, and has replies asking whether it could reduce fat under the cheekbones [4]. The posts are anecdotal and stated in the posters' own terms; they go beyond the clinical literature, which covers the submental region and body sites cleared by the FDA [1][8].

On T Nation, members have asked whether cryolipolysis would work on a stubborn spot while cutting [19], described it as a way to 'kill the cells so they can never refill' [20], and compared topical cold approaches with the commercial treatment [34].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org and T Nation, cryolipolysis is discussed as a possible way to remove facial, submental or stubborn body fat locally, with members debating whether it suits younger men with low body fat [4][19][20].

claims.claim: Freezing fat is a legitimate way to get local fat loss, even from the face.
claims.believers: The author of one looksmax.org thread describes it as a slower, non-invasive version of liposuction and argues that cooled fat tissue is cleared by the body. Replies ask about using it on cheek fat [4].
claims.experts: Reviews report modest reductions in fat-layer thickness in cleared areas with good safety, and the FDA has cleared it for the submental area and jawline among other sites; the published studies reviewed here do not cover cheek fat [1][2][8].

claims.claim: Cold causes white fat to convert to brown fat that burns off.
claims.believers: The same thread proposes that cold makes fat cells turn brown and burn calories to produce heat [4].
claims.experts: Published studies describe cryolipolysis as selective fat-cell injury followed by clearance, shown in a pig model, and a 2025 pilot trial has examined white-adipose conversion directly [5][6][21].

claims.claim: Treated fat cells are killed permanently, so they cannot refill.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster describes cryolipolysis as a way to kill the cells so they never refill [20].
claims.experts: Reviews describe the injured cells as removed by macrophages, producing a thinner local fat layer over time [15]; a split-body trial followed abdominal changes for 12 weeks [13].

claims.claim: An ice pack at home can do the same thing.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster in a topical fat-loss thread says fat cells die under a cold stimulus and that an ice pack and some time is enough [34].
claims.experts: The published studies concern controlled cooling with regulated devices of the kind cleared by the FDA; none of the studies reviewed here tests household ice [1][5]. Cold can injure skin, and cold panniculitis after cold exposure has been documented in children [35].

claims.believers: Marketing and forum posts emphasise the lack of surgery and downtime, and a 2023 review describes it as safe with minimal adverse effects [15].
claims.experts: Paradoxical adipose hyperplasia has been reported in about 0.12 to 1.0 percent of treatments, can require liposuction or abdominoplasty to correct, and was the subject of a high-profile lawsuit that was settled in 2022 [1][27].
